title: Bodhi Pakshika Dharma Retreat 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens the weekend retreat by reading a passage from Florence Caplow's research on the great women of the Zen lineage, which says the dharma cannot arise without the mountains, magpies, and flowing water. Nomon then tells of a shower knob that won't turn off, with its screwdrivers, a small crowbar, failing eyesight, and rising agitation, until a hidden cap over a screw comes to mind. The story becomes a way to retranslate the three poisons as desire and aversion, annoyance, and ignorance, and to describe freedom in the middle of illness, aging, and death. Nomon closes by reading the Buddha's last exhortation to monks and nuns, whose stated purpose reaches past the students to compassion for the whole world.

That might be, but it might also be that the silence and the ritual was the important part.
Think about that.

Assuming what's going to be important.
Makes you wonder, do you really know what's going to be important?
So if I say anything worthwhile this weekend, it's not for my own sort of personal power.
It's a coming together of circumstances in a beneficial way, including your effort and your presence.
And I have here a little invitation.
I want to read to you some words from an invitation because here we are at the beginning of our retreat, which is like an invitation into something.
This is the invitation to Florence Caplow's Choussot ceremony in the Bay Area at the end of the month.
And I think it's a quote from her research, *The Great Women of the Zen Lineage*.
So this is the quote:
*The dharma does not rise up alone.
It can't emerge without reliance on the world.
If I take up the challenge of speaking, I must surely borrow the form and the emptiness of the mountains and hills and the great earth, the call of the magpies and the cry of the crows.

This is important, actually, I think.

I said that.

And I like I told the story the other day here.
I think like for some reason when we were in the car, three kids and the parents in the car, I was very proud of usually being the first one who could read the signs in the distance.

Like I can read that.

I remembered that.
I had forgotten that.

So then I'm like, okay.

And then you're like kind of messing with a screwdriver.
And then I'm going to frustrate it again.
I can't get the little cap that might be there off.

Yes, I meant you could take one of those things.
So the Buddha noticed that the mind has three strong tendencies, which I don't know if he called them this.
Maybe it was called this later.
And I don't actually in this case, I didn't look up what the original sort of Buddhist language was, but the translation that ended up happening in English is very dark and intense.
Three poisons in the mind, three poisons in the mind.
So maybe it's not too unreasonable a phrase because, you know, in a way I was poisoning myself.
Trying to just take care of the simple household and very predictable challenge, right?
Do we think when we install these things that they're not going to break?
No, we know they're going to break, but we kind of think they won't break.
And so one of the things that happened as Buddhism came into English is some of the early translations just became dominant.

So maybe we'll come up with something better than the three poisons.

It rolls off the tongue.
Greed, hatred, and delusion.
So I thought we might retranslate these and start reflecting a little bit on our experience.
So instead of being sort of dire words, maybe applying to some other person or maybe on the extreme times in our life, there's something that might be unfolding all the time.
And the reason why it might be helpful to reflect on some of these teachings and find ways to describe them that has resonance for us.
The reason why that might be useful is because it might give us a more accurate and nuanced understanding of what's actually happening.
And if we understand a little more accurately what's actually happening, we might be able to do something about it and free ourselves from this, you know, whatever you want to call it, poison.
So I've been thinking maybe instead of greed, maybe it's better to say desire.
And we can include in desire aversion, which is kind of desire just in the other direction.
So this wanting of something, this wanting of something or wanting of not something to be happening comes up very frequently, doesn't it?
So we should study this, I think.
In my case, I had a strong desire to have the shower just turn off.
I was supposed to turn off and a great aversion to seeing something different with my eyes and with my ears than what I expected.
And so this was sort of activating in some way.
Maybe instead of hatred, which is like pretty extreme, we could just have annoyance, right?
I mean, it's a little more everyday, right?
Like in a given day, someone might ask you, "Did you have a lot of hatred today?
Were you annoyed about anything?"
Oh, yes.
That's maybe annoyance.
So, and these are closely coupled, right?
I had a desire for it to be different, sort of one aspect of the same situation.
And I had some annoyance, not wanting this, annoyed, you know, agitated, not settled, not at peace with the situation.
So annoyance or hatred seems to have this quality, doesn't it?
Sort of being unsettled.
And then what happens, too, is you can't think straight, right?
You can't think straight, which helps.
You keep looping around.
And there's all kinds of stuff we could study about stress physiology that starts kicking in.
Actually, it turns out parts of your brain activate aspects of your hormonal system, which actually suppress your prefrontal cortex.
You literally can't think straight.
It literally shuts down, you know.
The more annoyed you get, the less you can think straight.
This really does happen.
And then maybe in delusion, instead of delusion, which is a very sort of slippery and vague like delusion, you know, maybe just ignorance, you know, or confusion is another possibility.
So, but pretty obvious in my shower story, I was ignorant of the nature of a little shower knob.

I thought it was one way.
I took action based on my understanding, right?
As we do, you know.
Every time we make a decision or take action, it's based on some understanding of the way things are, right?
It's not just arbitrary.
We're smart people.
But what if the basis of our action is actually not right, is incorrect, is ignorance?
And, you know, this is a little bit of a silly story on purpose.

It's not just like, "ah ha ha."
Is that we maybe have a chance of seeing something?
Maybe we have a chance of seeing something when we study the biggest Buddhist teaching, you know, the overriding, huge Buddhist teaching in the middle of just ordinary, everyday phenomena.
Maybe that will increase our ability to be aware of these factors of mind when something a little more loaded happens, like we have an interpersonal interaction, for instance, of any kind.

A little bit of desire for this other person to be slightly different from the way they are.
A little bit of aversion to some aspect of them.

Have you noticed this?
You know how small of a thing can trigger some little story or some narrative or some aversion?
I like to study this at the gym, actually, especially if they have the headphones on or something.

You know what kind of person that is, right?
And you wish they were a little bit of a different way.
Why are they doing the stair machine like that?
They should do it a different way.
So all this stuff comes up often.

So the title of freedom is alluding to the possibility of a little more freedom in the middle of this human situation.

Like I think in America we tend to think freedom is like getting rid of something: getting rid of government, getting rid of responsibilities, getting rid of having lots of money, getting rid of work, right?
Getting rid of all kinds of things, getting rid of other colored people, anything.
So it's not what's meant in Buddhist practice.
Not a getting rid of, not a freedom from, but a freedom in, a freedom in the middle of.
So to be able to have shower knobs that break, people that aren't like us, and more serious things too, right?
Like illness, several people in the sangha aren't here tonight because they're ill.
And aging, which is all of us, and death, right?
So all these things are happening.

So the Buddha's sort of genius is what if it was possible not to sort of turn away from any of this or try to explain it away or figure out a way around it, like an end run, you know, into some other world or some other state, like in some kind of enlightened state where we don't feel anything, you know?

And in their cosmology they had other sort of levels of existence that were kind of like this, but they were seen as suffering worlds, you know, worlds where you're sort of like happy and blissed out all the time.
So that was not what he was interested in.

What he discovered through practice and study, and then I think probably understood a lot better over the course of 40 years of teaching, is that it's possible to be completely straightforward about this stuff, to know it deeply and be free in the middle of it.
Does that mean we'll never be annoyed?
I'm not sure.
Probably not.
Maybe we don't have to run this cycle so hard the way we do.
Maybe we don't have to suffer in the way we do when little things happen and then big things happen.

And so as the Buddha was dying, and I just thought about that part about I'm sure his understanding greatly deepened over the course of teaching, which is not the traditional way of telling the story of the Buddha, but I think that's probably the case, don't you?
The way this, the enthusiastic way the story of the Buddha is told is like he had this, you know, practiced really hard, right?

Maybe that's so, I don't know, but my experience has been you learn a lot better through teaching.
So I think he understood something very clearly and then explored it for the rest of his conventional life.

In the teaching that records the last days and months of his life, he made some recommendations for how to practice, how to take up this project of freedom.
So I want to read you a few paragraphs of the sutra on the Buddha's death.

*O monks and nuns, I say to you that these teachings of which I have direct knowledge and which have been made known to you, these you should thoroughly learn, cultivate, develop and frequently practice, so that the life of purity may be established and may long endure, for the welfare and happiness of the multitude and out of compassion for the world, to bring benefit, well-being and happiness to gods and humans.*
It's a long sentence.
I'll read that first paragraph again.

*O monks and nuns, I say to you that these teachings of which I have direct knowledge, which we will study this weekend, and which have been made known to you, these you should thoroughly learn, cultivate, develop and frequently practice, so that the life of purity may be established and may long endure, for the welfare and happiness of the multitude, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, well-being and happiness of gods and humans.*
And what, O monks and nuns, are these teachings?

They are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four constituents of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path.

These are the teachings of which I have direct knowledge, which I have made known to you, and which you should thoroughly learn, cultivate, develop and frequently practice, so that the life of purity may be established and may long endure, for the welfare and happiness of the multitude, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, well-being and happiness of gods and humans.
Then the Blessed One said to the monks and nuns, "I exhort you, I exhort you, all compound things are subject to vanish.
Strive with earnestness.
The time of the Tathagata's parinirvana is near.
Soon the Tathagata will utterly pass away."
Tathagata is another word for himself, for the Buddha.
I'm about to die, he's saying.
And having spoken these ones, the Happy One, I love that, that's the translation, the Happy One, the Great Master spoke again in verse.
*My ears are now full ripe, the life span is short.
Departing I go hence from you, relying on myself alone.
Be earnest then, O Bhikkhus, that's monks.
Be mindful and of virtue pure.
With firm resolve, guard your own mind.
Who so untiringly pursues the Dharma and the discipline shall go beyond the round of births and make an end to suffering.*
So that's our frame of teaching.
And a few things I think are really interesting in that, don't you think?
One thing that's interesting is the purpose that's laid out.
It's not just so that you people in front of me will be awakened or become Buddhas.
He doesn't say anything about anybody becoming Buddhas.
So he's not trying to generate Buddhas.
And he's not just trying to make his students be deeply happy, although that's certainly included.
The purpose is for the whole world.
Did you notice that?
For compassion for the world, for happiness for everyone.
So that's interesting.
Sometimes in Buddhist history, those sort of later schools of Buddhism say that their earlier schools were a little like narrow and didn't care about compassion, but compassion is right there.
So who knows?
Matter of emphasis.
So that's one thing that's interesting.
